summary: This RFC explains how Explicit Congestion Notification can be used with RTP over UDP, with RTCP as the feedback. It defines a new RTCP XR block, a new RTCP transport feedback message, and a STUN extension for optional initialization.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6679 explains how Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) traffic over UDP can use Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN). Receivers report congestion marks over RTCP so senders can react before congestion causes more packet loss.

questions: how to use ecn with rtp
how does rtp detect ecn path failure
subtitle: Use RTCP feedback to carry ECN congestion marks from RTP receivers back to senders.

tldr.problem: RTP over UDP has no built-in feedback for ECN marks. A sender therefore needs a way to learn that routers marked its packets for congestion.
tldr.mechanism: Receivers report ECN marks and packet counts in RTCP feedback and summary reports. SDP signals support, and the endpoints check that the path carries ECN correctly.
tldr.outcome: Senders treat ECN congestion marks like packet loss and monitor for paths that clear or drop marks. RFC 6679 is updated by RFC 8311.

facts.label: Minimum ECT probes
facts.value: 2 per RTCP reporting interval is recommended

today: RFC 6679 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2012. The unit metadata says RFC 8311 updates it.

sections.title: Why RTP Needs ECN Feedback
sections.content:
ECN lets a router mark a packet to report congestion instead of immediately discarding it. A transport sender must learn about those marks to adjust its traffic. UDP does not provide feedback, so RTP uses the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) to report what receivers observed.

RTP carries real-time media, where dropped packets can affect what users hear or see. This RFC defines RTCP feedback, checks that ECN works end to end, and signaling and procedures for starting ECN use.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can mark an IP packet to signal congestion rather than drop it. RTCP gives an RTP receiver a way to tell the sender about those marks.

sections.title: The Four Stages of ECN Use
sections.content:
The mechanism has four parts: negotiate ECN support, initiate and verify ECN, use ECN during the session, and detect failures with fallback. Both participants and the network path must support the marks; a middlebox may block or remove them even when endpoints support ECN.

After successful verification, the sender marks RTP data packets as ECN-capable. Receivers report what arrived. RTCP packets themselves MUST NOT be ECN-marked, so feedback can still get through when ECN-marked media packets fail.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints first agree to use ECN and check the path. They then mark media packets and send reports about the marks, while leaving RTCP unmarked.

sections.title: Urgent Feedback and Periodic Reports
sections.content:
The RTP/AVPF transport feedback packet carries timely ECN information, especially when a receiver sees an ECN-CE mark. It reports the highest RTP sequence number and cumulative counts for ECT(0), ECT(1), ECN-CE, not-ECT, lost, and duplicate packets.

The RTCP XR ECN Summary Report carries the same counters for regular reporting and path checks. Its block type is 13; its length must be a multiple of five words, and a receiver MUST discard a report with another length. The summary uses sequence information already present in the Sender or Receiver Report in the same compound RTCP packet.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver can send a quick report when it sees a congestion mark. It also sends regular totals so the sender can compare packet counts over time.

sections.title: Signaling Support in SDP
sections.content:
The media-level SDP attribute a=ecn-capable-rtp lists initiation methods in preference order: rtp, ice, or leap. The optional mode parameter describes whether an endpoint can set ECN marks, read them, or both. The ect parameter indicates a preferred ECT marking; ECT(0) is recommended.

With offer/answer SDP, the answer selects a supported method. If the answer omits the attribute, ECN MUST NOT be used in either direction. SDP also signals the RTCP feedback packet and XR summary block, and the optional ICE method uses the rtp+ecn ICE option.
sections.plainLanguage: SDP tells the other endpoint whether ECN can be sent, received, or both. The answer must confirm support before either direction uses ECN.

sections.title: Starting ECN and Reporting Congestion
sections.content:
The required initiation method sends a small fraction of RTP packets with ECT marks while leaving others unmarked. The RFC recommends at least two ECT-marked packets per RTCP reporting interval. Receivers report successful receipt, and the sender waits until the known participants have demonstrated support before marking all RTP data packets.

After initiation, a receiver that sees an ECN-CE mark or packet loss schedules feedback as soon as possible, unless timely feedback is unnecessary. By default, the sender's congestion-control algorithm treats an ECN-CE mark like packet loss. An optional STUN check with ICE can test the path before or alongside media transmission, and a leap-of-faith method is limited to controlled environments.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender first marks only some media packets to test the path. After receivers confirm they arrived with ECN information intact, the sender can mark all RTP data and respond to reported congestion.

sections.title: Detecting Failures and Falling Back
sections.content:
A route change may introduce a middlebox that drops ECN-marked packets or changes their marks to not-ECT. The sender compares the counts it sent with the receiver's ECT, ECN-CE, not-ECT, loss, and duplicate reports to identify a possible problem.

If ECT packets have unusually high loss, the sender SHOULD switch to not-ECT and check whether loss stops. If this indicates an ECN failure, the sender returns to initiation. It may retry later or renegotiate the session to disable ECN; repeated fallback after successful initiation is a reason to disable it.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender checks whether ECN-marked packets arrive as expected. If those packets disappear more often, it stops marking them and checks whether delivery improves.

sections.title: Security and Media Translators
sections.content:
False RTCP feedback can make a sender reduce its rate or disable ECN. The RFC recommends authenticating and integrity-protecting feedback and session signaling; encrypt RTCP if its loss and congestion details are sensitive. An on-path attacker that can change packets can alter ECN marks, which endpoints cannot prevent by themselves.

Translators that do not change media should copy ECN bits unchanged unless they are congested. A translator that combines or splits packets must update ECN markings and feedback counts. A transcoder or mixer runs separate ECN feedback loops and MUST NOT forward downstream ECN feedback upstream.
sections.plainLanguage: RTCP feedback and signaling need protection so an attacker cannot forge reports or remove ECN support. Translators must preserve or correctly update ECN information when they handle media packets.

items.title: ECT(0) and ECT(1)
items.text: Counts of packets received with each ECN-capable marking.

items.title: ECN-CE
items.text: Count of packets marked as experiencing congestion.

items.title: not-ECT
items.text: Count of packets received without ECN capability.

items.title: Lost and duplicate
items.text: Separate counts for missing packets and repeated packets.
